function.name: calculate_electric_current
function.description: Calculate the electric current through a conductor given voltage and resistance. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

voltage.description: The voltage across the conductor in Volts. This is a float type value.

resistance.description: The resistance of the conductor in Ohms. This is a float type value.

conductance.description: The conductance of the conductor in Siemens. Optional if resistance is provided. Default: 0.3 This is a float type value.

message.content:
Electricity isn’t the discovery of a single person—it’s the culmination of observations and experiments that span millennia. Here’s a quick timeline of key figures who helped uncover the nature of electricity:

| Era | Key Person | Contribution |
|-----|------------|--------------|
| **Ancient Greece** | Thales of Miletus (c. 600 BCE) | First recorded observation of static electricity by rubbing amber (Greek *elektron*). |
| **17th Century** | William Gilbert (1544–1603) | Published *De Magnete* (1600), coined the term “electricus” for amber’s attraction, and distinguished magnetism from static electricity. |
| **18th Century** | Otto von Guericke (1602–1686) | Demonstrated static electricity with his famous “magnetic storm” experiments. |
| **18th Century** | Benjamin Franklin (1706–1790) | Conducted kite‑experiment (1752), introduced the concepts of positive/negative charge, and proposed the conservation of charge. |
| **19th Century** | Alessandro Volta (1745–1827) | Invented the voltaic pile (early battery) in 1800, providing a steady source of electric current. |
| **19th Century** | Michael Faraday (1791–1867) | Discovered electromagnetic induction (1831) and formulated Faraday’s laws of induction. |
| **19th Century** | James Clerk Maxwell (1831–1879) | Unified electricity and magnetism into Maxwell’s equations (1860s). |

So while no single individual “discovered” electricity, the collective work of these pioneers—and many others—led to our modern understanding of electric phenomena.
